entities.title: The computer's names differ between the client and the server
entities.summary: shared/protocol.ts LEVELS calls strengths 2, 6 and 8 Weekend Wood, County Champ and The Machine; the client, the README and UI-DESIGN.md call them Weekend Player, County Champion and Stockfish.
entities.expected: A game against the computer shows the same opponent name while it is played and afterwards in the history, as UI-DESIGN.md names the strengths.
entities.observed: During play the client names the opponent from Main.LEVELS ("Stockfish · Weekend Player"); once the finished game is saved, the Worker names it from LEVELS in shared/protocol.ts (db.ts player(): "Stockfish · Weekend Wood"), so the history and replay show the other name. The blurbs differ too, though only the client shows them.
reproduction: Signed in, play the computer at strength 2, 6 or 8 to the end
acceptanceCriteria: shared/protocol.ts LEVELS and godot/scripts/main.gd LEVELS give the same names, matching docs/UI-DESIGN.md.

origin.description: LEVELS, compared with Main.LEVELS in godot/scripts/main.gd and the README's table.

entities.title: rules.ts still describes a browser that no longer uses it
entities.summary: rules.ts opens by saying it is shared by the browser and the server; since the Godot client has its own rules, describe(), scoreFor() and START_FEN are used only by the tests.
entities.compromise: The first, TypeScript version of the game ran these rules in the browser; the Godot client replaced it, and the helpers it used stayed.
entities.cost: A reader trusts that the client and the server judge a game with the same code, which is no longer true (see godot/chess backlog two-rule-sets), and keeps unused helpers in step.
acceptanceCriteria: rules.ts says who uses it, and helpers nothing but their own tests use are gone or used.

origin.description: The file's opening comment, against what imports it.
